analysis.one_liner: Toughens mine safety enforcement, protects whistle-blowing miners, and extends workplace-safety law to government employees.
analysis.headline: Introduced 11 days before the 117th Congress ended, the mine safety bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal mine safety law to give investigators more power to find out why mine accidents happen, including an independent panel for disasters with three or more deaths. It would raise penalties sharply — a mine operator who knowingly violates safety standards could face up to five years in prison and a $1 million fine — and double fines for mines with repeated violations. It would strengthen protections for miners who report hazards, require underground coal mines to install atmospheric monitoring systems and brief miners on conditions before each shift, and extend the Occupational Safety and Health Act to government employees, who are currently not covered by it.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners, especially those in underground mines, gain stronger legal protection when they report dangerous conditions, guaranteed pay when a safety order closes part of a mine, better pre-shift briefings on hazards, and required training on their rights. Families of miners killed in disasters would get findings from an independent investigation panel. State and local government workers — roughly eight million people who have no OSHA coverage today — would gain federal workplace-safety protections for the first time.

how_it_helps.text: Requires an independent investigation panel, with subpoena power and conflict-of-interest rules, for any mine accident involving three or more deaths, and requires the Labor Department to determine why each accident happened and refer possible crimes to the Attorney General.
Allows inspectors and investigators to interview miners privately, away from the operator and its lawyers, and lets miners' representatives take part in accident investigations.

Raises penalties: a knowing safety violation becomes a felony with up to five years in prison and a $1 million fine; mines with a pattern of violations face doubled civil penalties; officers and directors who knowingly order violations can be held personally liable.

Rewrites whistle-blower protections so miners cannot be fired or disciplined for reporting hazards, refusing unsafe work, or reporting injuries, with a path to quick reinstatement and back pay, and bans forced arbitration waivers of those rights.

Requires underground coal mines to install atmospheric monitoring systems tracking methane, oxygen, and carbon monoxide, to brief every miner on current conditions before they enter the work area, and to meet higher rock-dust standards that limit explosive coal dust.
Extends the Occupational Safety and Health Act to government employees and expands retaliation protections and victims' rights under that law.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, their officers and directors, and independent contractors at mines. They would face criminal exposure for knowingly unsafe operations, doubled civil penalties at mines with repeated violations, withdrawal orders forcing miners out until plans are fixed, required monitoring and communication equipment, certification and training costs, and interest on late penalty payments.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall heavily on mine operators — atmospheric monitoring systems, direct-reading dust monitors, certification fees, and expanded training all carry real expense in an industry already under cost pressure, and some of that cost would be passed on in coal prices.

The bill widens criminal liability to officers and directors personally and raises prison exposure to ten years for repeat reckless violations, which operators and their trade associations would argue deters investment and over-criminalizes workplace conduct.

Extending OSHA to state and local government employees would impose new inspection, recordkeeping, and abatement obligations on public employers, including small towns and school districts that have never operated under federal safety enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits run to people in one of the country's most dangerous occupations and to millions of government workers with no federal safety coverage; the costs fall on the companies that profit from mining and, in part, on coal prices. Stronger enforcement and whistle-blower protection address failures that have repeatedly surfaced in mine disasters, and the bill includes cost-containment features such as payment plans for operators who cannot pay penalties. The main honest trade-off is real compliance and litigation expense for operators against protections that only bind them when safety is actually at risk.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Casey introduced the bill on December 22, 2022; the Senate sent it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day, and with the Congress ending on January 3, 2023, no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey of Pennsylvania introduced the Robert C. Byrd Mine Safety Protection Act of 2022 on December 22, 2022, joined by Senators Sherrod Brown and Joe Manchin.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the only action the bill ever received; the complete action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill's cosponsor list totaled just two senators beyond the sponsor, both Democrats, out of a Senate with 48 Democrats, 2 independents, and 50 Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off: they avoid the criminal penalties, doubled fines, withdrawal orders, monitoring requirements, and expanded whistle-blower rules the bill would have imposed, and government employers avoid new OSHA obligations. Miners and their families gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal mine operators and their officers

for.name: Sen. Robert P. Casey, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on December 22, 2022.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral; no action scheduled
against.what_they_did: Took no further action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — in the 11 days before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only three senators — all Democrats — are on record either way, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the fight was never tested.

industries.industry: Coal mining companies and their officers
industries.note: The bill would expose operators and personally their directors and officers to criminal penalties up to five years in prison and $1 million fines, double civil penalties at mines with patterns of violations, withdrawal orders for unpaid penalties or revoked plans, and stronger retaliation claims from miners. Avoiding these rules was the payoff of the bill dying in committee.

industries.industry: Mine safety monitoring and equipment makers
industries.note: Required atmospheric monitoring systems, approved direct-reading coal dust explosibility monitors, and electronic records systems would create a mandated market for safety equipment. Their interest runs alongside miners' safety.

Extending OSHA to government employees would subject public employers to federal inspections, recordkeeping, and penalties. The cost to them is the gain in protection for millions of uncovered public-sector workers.
